mainTopic: שאלה בבעלים, and the Torah sources for the rules of the four שומרים
overview: This amud finishes the משנה's rule about שאלה בבעלים. If the cow was borrowed first and the owner only afterward, the borrower must pay when the cow dies. The גמרא reads 'the owner with it' as meaning both borrowings happened at the same moment, and it shows two ways that can happen. Then it quotes the משנה of the four שומרים and finds the Torah source for each one's rules. It proves that the second פרשה is about the שומר שכר, because paying the קרן with no way out by oath is stricter than כפל. Next it asks where we learn that a שומר שכר pays for loss: from the doubled verb ״גָּנוֹב יִגָּנֵב״, or from a קל וחומר. Finally it looks for the source that a שואל pays when the animal is captured, and settles on רבי נתן's reading of the word ״או״. This leads into the argument between רבי יאשיה and רבי יונתן about how to read 'and' in a פסוק, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Cow first, owner later: the borrower must pay
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that if someone borrowed the cow first and only afterward borrowed or hired its owner, he is חייב when the cow dies. It learns this from the פסוק 'בעליו אין עמו שלם ישלם'.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if he borrowed the cow first and afterward borrowed or hired the owner, and the cow died, he must pay. The פסוק says: 'If its owner is not with him, he shall surely pay.'
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives the opposite case to the one it just discussed. Here the owner was not 'with' the cow at the moment it was borrowed, so the borrower must pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The exemption of בעליו עמו only works if the owner was already working for the borrower when the cow was borrowed. Here the borrowing of the cow came first, and at that moment the owner was not 'with him.' So the normal rule for a שואל applies, and he pays.

keyTerms.meaning: Its owner is not with him: the case where the borrower must pay

steps.whyThisMatters: The order of events decides the outcome. The owner must be working for the borrower at the moment the borrowing of the cow starts.

phrases.english: But if he borrowed the cow
and afterward borrowed the owner,
phrases.notes: 'Borrowing the owner' means getting the owner to work for you for free.

phrases.english: or hired him, and the cow died, he is liable,
as it is said: "If its owner is not with him,
he shall surely pay."

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲבָל שָׁאַל אֶת הַפָּרָה וְאַחַר כָּךְ שָׁאַל אֶת הַבְּעָלִים
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the cow was borrowed before the owner was borrowed or hired, the borrower is liable when it dies.

steps.title: Reading 'with it' as 'at the exact same moment'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notices that the משנה has a separate case of 'owner first, then cow.' From this it concludes that the first case, 'the owner with it,' must mean both happened at exactly the same time.
steps.simpleTranslation: Since the later clause teaches 'and afterward he borrowed the cow,' we learn that when the first clause says 'with it,' it means literally together, at the same moment.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens its discussion of the משנה by drawing an inference from its wording. This sets up the question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If 'with it' could include 'owner first, then cow,' the משנה would not need a separate clause for that case. So 'with it' must mean something else: both borrowings happened at the same instant.

keyTerms.meaning: The Talmudic discussion of the משנה
The later clause of a משנה
The first clause of a משנה
It follows that, we can infer
Literally together with it, at the same moment

phrases.english: Gemara
From the fact that the latter clause teaches:
"and afterward he borrowed the cow,"
it follows that the first clause, which teaches "with it,"
means literally with it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא by reading the wording of the משנה closely.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'With it' in the רישא means the owner and the cow were borrowed at the same instant.

steps.title: How can both happen at the same moment?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how the owner and the cow could ever be borrowed at exactly the same time. The cow is acquired by משיכה, while the owner's services start as soon as they are agreed in words.
steps.simpleTranslation: Literally together? Can you find such a case? The cow is acquired by pulling, but the owner by speaking!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the reading it just made. It says the 'same moment' case seems impossible.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Words take effect right away, but the cow only becomes borrowed once the borrower pulls it. So the owner would always be borrowed first, which is the סיפא's case. That would leave the רישא with no possible case.

keyTerms.meaning: Can you find such a case?
Pulling, a way of taking possession of an animal

phrases.english: Literally with it?
Can you find such a case?
The cow is acquired by pulling,
and the owner by speaking!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the inference of step 2 by asking whether such a case is possible.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading that 'with it' means at the exact same moment.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Different ways of acquiring take effect at different times. Speech works at once and pulling comes later, so 'same moment' seems impossible.

steps.title: First answer: the cow is already in the borrower's yard
steps.stepSummary: The cow is standing in the borrower's חצר. His courtyard acquires it for him, so no משיכה is needed, and both borrowings take effect together when they agree.
steps.simpleTranslation: If you want, say: for example, where the cow is standing in the borrower's courtyard, so it does not need pulling.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question with a case where the cow does not need to be pulled at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A person's חצר can acquire things for him. If the cow is already there, the borrowing of the cow happens through the agreement itself, at the same moment as the owner's services begin.

keyTerms.meaning: If you want, say: introduces a possible answer
His courtyard, which can acquire things for him
Does not need, is not missing

phrases.english: If you want, say:
for example, where the cow is standing
in the borrower's courtyard,
so it does not need pulling.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: כְּגוֹן דְּקַיְימָא פָּרָה בַּחֲצֵרוֹ דְּשׁוֹאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Defines a specific case that removes the timing gap.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Pulling is always needed, so the cow is always borrowed after the owner.
steps.terutzMaskana: When the cow is in the borrower's חצר, both borrowings begin at once.

steps.title: Second answer: the owner's service is delayed until the pulling
steps.stepSummary: Another answer: the borrower tells the owner that his services will only begin when the cow is pulled. That way both borrowings start at the same moment.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or if you want, say: where he said to him, 'You yourself will not be borrowed until the moment your cow is pulled.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second, different way to solve the same problem.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the cow still needs pulling. Instead, the agreement for the owner's services is set to take effect only at the moment of משיכה, so the two line up exactly.
steps.whatToRemember: 'בעליו עמו' in the רישא means the owner and the cow were borrowed at the same moment. This is possible if the cow is in the borrower's חצר, or if the owner's service is set to start at the moment the cow is pulled.

phrases.english: Or if you want, say:
where he said to him:
"You yourself will not be borrowed
until the moment your cow is pulled."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, separate answer to the קשיא of step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Delays the owner's agreement so it matches the moment of pulling.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Speech always takes effect before the pulling.
steps.terutzMaskana: The parties can set the owner's service to begin exactly at the משיכה.

steps.title: New topic: the four kinds of guardians
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a משנה from earlier: there are four types of שומרים: שומר חנם, שואל, נושא שכר, and שוכר.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned there: there are four guardians: an unpaid guardian, a borrower, a paid guardian, and a renter.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new discussion by quoting an earlier משנה. This is a setup line for the analysis that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing is being argued yet. The list of four שומרים is laid out as the base text the גמרא will now examine.

keyTerms.meaning: We learned in a משנה elsewhere

phrases.english: We learned there:
phrases.notes: This refers to the משנה on דף צג.

phrases.english: There are four guardians:
an unpaid guardian and the borrower,
a paid guardian and the renter.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the בעליו עמו discussion and opens a new topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: There are four types of שומרים: unpaid, borrower, paid, and renter.

steps.title: What each of the four guardians swears or pays
steps.stepSummary: The משנה continues: a שומר חנם swears for everything, a שואל pays for everything, and a שומר שכר and a שוכר swear for injured, captured or dead animals but pay for loss and theft.
steps.simpleTranslation: An unpaid guardian swears about everything. A borrower pays for everything. A paid guardian and a renter swear about an injured, captured or dead animal, and they pay for something lost or stolen.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes quoting the משנה it began in Step 6. Now it gives the actual rules for each of the four שומרים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are three levels of responsibility. A שומר חנם is the most lenient: he swears and goes free. A שואל is the strictest: he always pays. The שומר שכר and שוכר are in the middle: they go free for accidents beyond their control, but they pay for theft and loss.

keyTerms.meaning: Swears an oath that the loss happened the way he says, and then he is free from paying
An animal that was injured or broken
An animal that was captured, for example by raiders
Loss and theft. These are things the guardian could have prevented by watching more carefully
A renter, someone who pays to use an item

steps.whatToRemember: שומר חנם swears for all. שואל pays for all. שומר שכר and שוכר swear for accidents but pay for theft and loss.
steps.confusionAlert: The oath is not a punishment. Swearing is how the guardian frees himself from paying.

phrases.english: An unpaid guardian swears about everything,
and the borrower pays for everything,
a paid guardian and the renter:

phrases.aramaic: נִשְׁבָּעִין עַל הַשְּׁבוּרָה וְעַל הַשְּׁבוּיָה וְעַל הַמֵּתָה,
phrases.english: they swear about the injured, about the captured, and about the dead animal,
and they pay for the lost item and for the stolen item.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the quote of the משנה that Step 6 began
steps.mimraCoreRuling: שומר חנם swears for all. שואל pays for all. שומר שכר and שוכר swear for accidents and pay for theft and loss.

steps.title: Where do these rules come from?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the Torah source of these four sets of rules.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where do we know these things?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the source of the משנה's rules. This sets up the next step, which brings a ברייתא as the answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה gave clear rules, but it did not show where in the Torah they come from. The גמרא wants to connect each rule to its פסוקים.

keyTerms.meaning: From where are these things known? A standard request for the source of a law

phrases.english: From where are these matters derived?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the rules quoted in Step 7
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The Torah source for the different rules of each שומר

steps.title: Three Torah passages for three guardians
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that the first פרשה is about a שומר חנם, the second is about a שומר שכר, and the third is about a שואל.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: the first passage was said about an unpaid guardian, the second about a paid guardian, and the third about a borrower.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a ברייתא. It splits the Torah's section on guardians into three passages and assigns each one to a different guardian.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The section in שמות 22 has three parts, and each part gives different rules. Once we know which guardian each part is about, we know where each rule in the משנה comes from.

keyTerms.meaning: A passage or section of the Torah

phrases.english: As the Sages taught:
the first passage was stated about an unpaid guardian,
phrases.notes: These are the three sections in שמות 22:6–14.

phrases.english: the second, about a paid guardian,
the third, about a borrower.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 8
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The three פרשיות in the Torah match שומר חנם, שומר שכר and שואל, in that order

steps.title: Why not switch the first two passages?
steps.stepSummary: The third passage clearly speaks about a borrower. But nothing says the first passage is about the unpaid guardian and the second about the paid one, so maybe it is the other way around.
steps.simpleTranslation: It makes sense that the third passage is about a borrower, because it says so clearly: 'And when a man borrows from his neighbor and it is injured or dies, if its owner is not with him, he shall surely pay.' But why say the first is about an unpaid guardian and the second about a paid guardian? I could say the opposite!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא accepts part of the ברייתא and challenges the rest. The third passage says 'borrow' in its own words, but the first two passages never say which guardian they mean.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'borrows' proves the third passage is about a שואל. The first two passages give no such label. So the ברייתא's order for them looks like a guess, and the גמרא says it could just as easily be reversed.

keyTerms.meaning: It is fine / granted. It accepts one part before challenging another part

phrases.english: Granted, the third is about a borrower, since it is stated clearly:
"And when a man borrows from his neighbor
and it is injured or dies,
its owner not being with him, he shall surely pay."
But the first about an unpaid guardian
and the second about a paid guardian? I could reverse it!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges how the ברייתא of Step 9 assigns the first two passages
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's claim that the first passage is about a שומר חנם and the second is about a שומר שכר
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Only the third passage names its guardian. Nothing in the first two passages forces this order, so they could be reversed.

steps.title: The second passage is stricter, so it fits the paid guardian
steps.stepSummary: It makes sense that the second passage is about a שומר שכר, because it makes him pay for theft and loss. That is a stricter rule, and it fits the guardian who is being paid.
steps.simpleTranslation: It stands to reason that the second passage is about a paid guardian, since in it he must pay for theft and loss.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the ברייתא's order with a logical reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A paid guardian should carry more responsibility than an unpaid one. The second passage makes the guardian pay for theft and loss, which is a strict rule. So it fits the שומר שכר.

keyTerms.meaning: It stands to reason / it makes sense

phrases.english: It stands to reason that the second is about a paid guardian,
since he is liable for theft and loss.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 10
steps.terutzResolutionType: Logical reasoning: the stricter passage belongs to the guardian who is being paid
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The order of the first two passages is arbitrary and could be reversed
steps.terutzMaskana: The second passage has the stricter rule of paying for theft and loss, so it belongs to the שומר שכר

steps.title: The first passage has its own strict rule
steps.stepSummary: On the contrary: the first passage has a strict rule too. It gives double payment for falsely claiming a thief took the item. So maybe the first passage is about the שומר שכר.
steps.simpleTranslation: On the contrary! The first passage is about a paid guardian, since in it he pays double when he falsely claims that a thief took the item.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the reason it just gave. It points out a strict rule in the first passage as well, so the same logic would make the first passage the paid guardian's.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule 'the stricter passage goes to the paid guardian' works in both directions. The second passage has paying for theft and loss, and the first passage has the double-payment penalty. So the reasoning of Step 11 does not settle the question yet.

keyTerms.meaning: Double payment, the fine a thief normally pays
Claims that a thief took it, when really he took it himself

phrases.english: On the contrary: the first is about a paid guardian,
since he pays double payment
when he makes the claim of a thief!
phrases.notes: He claims a thief stole it, but it turns out he kept it himself. See שמות 22:6–8.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Pushes back on the reasoning of Step 11
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The claim that only the second passage is the strict one
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The first passage also has a strict rule, the double payment for falsely claiming theft. So the reasoning could put the paid guardian in the first passage instead.

steps.title: Paying the principal without an oath is the stricter rule
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא defends its reading. Having to pay the קרן with no option of an oath is stricter than having to pay כפל only after a false oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even so, having to pay the principal with no chance to swear is stricter than paying double, which only happens through an oath.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 12. Yes, the first פרשה has כפל, but the second פרשה's rule is still the stricter one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first פרשה, the guardian pays כפל only if he swears falsely that a thief took the item. If he does not swear, he pays nothing extra. In the second פרשה, the guardian must pay for theft no matter what, and no oath can free him. That is the harsher rule, so the second פרשה belongs to the שומר שכר.

keyTerms.meaning: The principal: the actual value of the item

phrases.english: Even so,
paying the principal without an oath
is greater than double payment that comes with an oath.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the counterpoint of step 12 and restores the conclusion of step 11.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Comparing how strict each rule really is
steps.terutzHavaAmina: כפל is the harsher rule, so the first פרשה might be about the שומר שכר.
steps.terutzMaskana: Paying the קרן with no escape by oath is harsher, so the second פרשה is about the שומר שכר.

steps.title: Proof from the borrower, who pays only the principal
steps.stepSummary: The שואל gets all the benefit and is the strictest guardian, yet he pays only קרן. This shows that paying the קרן is the mark of the stricter guardian.
steps.simpleTranslation: Know that this is so: a borrower gets all the benefit, and still he pays only the principal.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings support for step 13 from the case of the שואל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The שואל gets all the benefit, so the Torah makes him the most liable guardian. Even so, his liability is paying the קרן, not כפל. So the strictest level of liability is measured by paying the קרן, not by כפל.

keyTerms.meaning: Know that this is so: a word that opens a supporting proof

phrases.english: Know that this is so,
for a borrower, all the benefit is his,
and he pays only the principal.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the claim made in step 13.
steps.raayaObject: That paying the קרן without an oath is stricter than כפל
steps.raayaSupportSource: The rules of the שואל, the strictest guardian, who pays only קרן

steps.title: Does the borrower really get all the benefit? He must feed the animal
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the proof. A borrowed animal needs food, so the borrower does have a cost.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does the borrower really get all the benefit? But the animal needs food!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the claim from step 14 that the borrower gets 'all the benefit.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the borrower has to pay for the animal's food, the deal is not pure benefit for him. That weakens the idea that he is a guardian who only gains.

keyTerms.meaning: But isn't it so...: opens a challenge

phrases.english: And does the borrower get all the benefit?
But the animal needs food!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהַשּׁוֹאֵל כׇּל הֲנָאָה שֶׁלּוֹ? וְהָא בָּעֲיָא מְזוֹנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the basis of the proof in step 14.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that a שואל gets all the benefit
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Feeding the animal is a cost to the borrower, so he does not get only benefit.

steps.title: The animal grazes in a marsh
steps.stepSummary: The case is one where the animal stands in a marsh and eats there for free.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a case where the animal stands in a marsh.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that we can picture an animal that finds its own food.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An animal in a marsh eats the grass there, and the borrower pays nothing for it. The borrower still has all the rules of a שואל, so the claim of 'all the benefit' holds in that case.

phrases.english: Where it stands in a marsh.
phrases.notes: There is free grass there, so the borrower spends nothing on food.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the food challenge of step 15.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The borrower always has to pay for food.
steps.terutzMaskana: In a case where the animal grazes freely, there is no cost, and he is still a שואל.

steps.title: But the animal needs guarding
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes further. Even with free food, the borrower must still watch the animal, and that is a burden.
steps.simpleTranslation: But the animal needs guarding!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second challenge to the 'all the benefit' claim.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Guarding takes effort, so the borrower is still giving something. The marsh answer solved food but not this.

phrases.english: But it needs guarding!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows the answer of step 16 with a new problem.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that a שואל gets all the benefit
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Guarding is an effort the borrower must make, so he does not get only benefit.

steps.title: The borrower is a city guard
steps.stepSummary: The case is one where the borrower is a city guard. He is already watching anyway, so guarding the animal costs him nothing extra.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a case where he is a city guard.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that we can picture a borrower who does no extra guarding.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A city guard is already watching the whole town. Guarding the borrowed animal adds no new work for him, so in that case he truly gets all the benefit.

phrases.english: When he is a city guard.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the guarding challenge of step 17.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every borrower must put in effort to guard.
steps.terutzMaskana: A city guard who borrows has no extra effort, and he is still a שואל.

steps.title: Second answer: say 'most of the benefit'
steps.stepSummary: A different answer: change the wording. The borrower gets most of the benefit, not all of it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or if you want, say: don't say 'all the benefit is his,' but say 'most of the benefit is his.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another way to answer steps 15 and 17. It does not look for a special case. It just softens the wording.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Food and guarding are small costs next to the free use of the animal. Getting most of the benefit is already enough reason to give the borrower the strictest liability.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say: introduces another answer

phrases.english: And if you want, say:
don't say 'all the benefit is his,'
rather say 'most of the benefit is his.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second answer to the challenges, in place of the specific cases in steps 16 and 18.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The borrower's position rests on getting 100% of the benefit.
steps.terutzMaskana: Getting most of the benefit is enough.

steps.title: Third answer: borrowing utensils
steps.stepSummary: Another answer: think of borrowed utensils. They need no food and almost no care.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or if you want, say: it is about borrowing utensils.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a third answer. When the borrowed item is a utensil, the challenges about food and guarding do not come up at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A borrowed utensil does not eat and needs no special watching. A שואל of utensils truly gets all the benefit, so the proof in step 14 stands.
steps.whatToRemember: The second פרשה is the שומר שכר, because paying the קרן with no way out by oath is stricter than כפל. The proof is the שואל, who is the strictest guardian and pays only קרן.

phrases.english: And if you want, say:
it is about borrowing utensils.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third answer to the challenges about food and guarding.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every borrowed item has upkeep costs.
steps.terutzMaskana: Borrowed utensils have no upkeep, so the borrower gets all the benefit.

steps.title: The משנה: the paid guardian and the renter
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the next line of the משנה. The paid guardian and the renter swear when the animal is injured, captured, or dead, but they pay for loss and theft.
steps.simpleTranslation: A paid guardian and a renter swear about an injured, captured, or dead animal, and they pay for a lost or stolen one.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the משנה and quotes its line about the נושא שכר and the שוכר. This sets up the discussion that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For accidents beyond their control, these two guardians take an oath and go free. For loss and theft, which careful guarding could have prevented, they must pay. The שוכר is treated the same as the שומר שכר.

phrases.english: A paid guardian and a renter swear

phrases.aramaic: עַל הַשְּׁבוּרָה וְעַל הַשְּׁבוּיָה וְעַל הַמֵּתָה,
phrases.english: about an injured animal, a captured one, and a dead one,
and they pay for loss and for theft.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the discussion about the sources and returns to quote the next part of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A שומר שכר and a שוכר go free by oath for accidents, but they pay for loss and theft.

steps.title: Theft has a verse, but where is loss written?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא accepts that theft has a clear source in the Torah and asks where the source for loss is.
steps.simpleTranslation: Theft is fine, because the Torah says 'If it is stolen from him, he must pay its owner.' But for loss, where do we learn it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is asking for the source of the משנה's rule from Step 21 that a שומר שכר pays for a lost animal. It sets up the search for a verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse openly mentions only theft (גניבה). The משנה also makes the guardian pay for loss (אבידה), and nothing in the verse says that directly. So the גמרא needs to find where that part comes from.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we know this?

phrases.english: Granted, theft,
as it is written:
"If it is stolen from him,
he must pay its owner."
But loss, from where do we know it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the Torah source of the משנה line quoted in Step 21.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The Torah source that a שומר שכר must pay for loss.

steps.title: The doubled verb includes loss
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא learns from the doubled wording ״גָּנוֹב יִגָּנֵב״ that the guardian pays for loss too.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא teaches: 'If it is stolen' would teach only theft. Where do we learn loss? The verse says ״גָּנוֹב יִגָּנֵב״, a doubled word, to teach that he pays in any case.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a ברייתא. The extra, doubled word in the verse adds loss to theft.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The Torah could have said the verb once. Since it says it twice, the ברייתא reads the extra word as adding a case. 'In any case' means the guardian pays whether the animal was stolen or lost.

keyTerms.meaning: In any case / no matter how

steps.whatToRemember: Loss is learned from the doubled verb ״גָּנוֹב יִגָּנֵב״: the extra word adds loss to theft.

phrases.english: As it is taught in a ברייתא:
"If it is stolen":
I would know only theft;
from where do we learn loss?
The verse says: "ganov yiganev,"
phrases.notes: The key is that the verb is doubled: 'stolen, it is stolen.'

phrases.english: meaning: in any case.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 22.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The doubled verb ״גָּנוֹב יִגָּנֵב״ teaches that loss is included.

steps.title: What about the view that a doubled verb is just normal speech?
steps.stepSummary: The proof works only for those who learn from doubled words. For those who say the Torah speaks like people do, the source for loss is gone.
steps.simpleTranslation: This works for the one who says we do not say 'the Torah speaks in human language.' But for the one who says we do say it, what is the source?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the proof from Step 23. One opinion holds that a doubled verb is just a normal way of speaking, so for that opinion nothing extra is taught.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule דברה תורה כלשון בני אדם means the Torah sometimes uses everyday style, like repeating a verb for emphasis. If you hold that rule, ״גָּנוֹב יִגָּנֵב״ is only style and cannot add loss. So that opinion still needs a source.

keyTerms.meaning: This works well for the one who says…
The Torah spoke the way people speak

steps.confusionAlert: Both opinions agree that a שומר שכר pays for loss. The argument is only about where that law comes from.

phrases.english: This works well for the one who says:
we do not say
that the Torah spoke in the language of people.
But for the one who says:

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרִינַן דִּבְּרָה תוֹרָה כִלְשׁוֹן בְּנֵי אָדָם,
phrases.english: we do say that the Torah spoke in the language of people,
what can be said?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the proof of Step 23 according to one opinion.
steps.kashyaTarget: The derivation of loss from the doubled verb.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Those who say the Torah speaks like people do read the doubled verb as style, so it cannot teach loss.

steps.title: In ארץ ישראל they learn loss from a קל וחומר
steps.stepSummary: Theft is close to an accident and he still pays, so loss, which is close to carelessness, surely makes him pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: They say in the West: it is a קל וחומר. If for theft, which is close to an accident, he pays, then for loss, which is close to carelessness, all the more so!
steps.whatsHappening: The scholars of ארץ ישראל give the other opinion a source without the doubled verb. They use logic, a קל וחומר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A theft is often hard to stop, so it is near to אונס. A loss usually happens because the guardian was not careful enough, so it is near to פשיעה. If the Torah makes him pay for the milder case, he surely pays for the more blameworthy one.

keyTerms.meaning: In the West, meaning ארץ ישראל
Logic from a lighter case to a stricter one

steps.whatToRemember: For the view that the Torah speaks like people do, loss comes from a קל וחומר: theft is near to אונס, and loss is near to פשיעה.

phrases.english: They say in the West:
it is learned with a קל וחומר:
if theft, which is close to an accident,
he pays,
then loss, which is close to carelessness,
is it not all the more so!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 24 with a new source.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Alternative source: logic instead of reading the verse closely
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Without the doubled verb, there would be no source for paying for loss.
steps.terutzMaskana: Loss is learned from theft by קל וחומר.

steps.title: Why the other opinion still needs the verse
steps.stepSummary: If a קל וחומר works, why does the first opinion use the verse? Because sometimes the Torah writes out a law even when logic could teach it.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other opinion? Something that can be learned by a קל וחומר, the verse still takes the trouble to write.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא briefly asks why the first opinion needs a verse if logic already teaches loss, and answers in the same line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One could argue that once a קל וחומר exists, the doubled verb is not needed for loss. The answer is that the Torah sometimes writes out a law that could be learned from logic. So the first opinion can still read the doubled verb as teaching loss.

keyTerms.meaning: The verse took the trouble to write it

steps.whatToRemember: Both opinions agree that a שומר שכר pays for loss. They differ only on the source: the doubled verb or a קל וחומר.

phrases.english: And the other opinion?
Something that can be learned with a קל וחומר,
the verse takes the trouble and writes it anyway.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִידַּךְ, מִילְּתָא דְּאָתְיָא בְּקַל וְחוֹמֶר טָרַח וְכָתַב לַהּ קְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends the first opinion's use of the verse after Step 25's קל וחומר.
steps.terutzResolutionType: General principle: the Torah sometimes writes out what logic could teach
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since a קל וחומר exists, the verse should not be needed to teach loss.
steps.terutzMaskana: The Torah sometimes writes a law even when a קל וחומר could teach it, so the first opinion can still learn from the verse.

steps.title: Where do we learn that a borrower pays for a captured animal?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה that the שואל pays for everything. Injury and death are written in the Torah for a borrower, so it asks for the source for capture.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says the borrower pays for everything. Fine, injury and death are written in the verse about a borrower. But where do we learn that a borrower pays when the animal is captured?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic, the borrower. It asks where the Torah teaches that he pays when the animal is captured.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse about a שואל lists only נשבר (injured) and מת (died). The משנה says he pays for everything, which includes שבויה (captured). So the גמרא needs a source for capture.

keyTerms.meaning: A borrower, who uses the item for free

phrases.english: And the borrower pays for everything.
Granted, for an animal that was injured or died,
as it is written:
"And if a man borrows from his fellow
and it is injured or dies."
But for a captured animal, with a borrower, from where do we know it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the topic of the guardian paying for theft and loss, and opens the next line of the משנה about the borrower.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A Torah source that a שואל pays when the animal is captured.

steps.title: Capture cannot be learned from injury and death
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests learning capture from injury and death. It rejects this, because injury and death are accidents people expect, while capture is a surprise.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might say: learn capture from injury and death. But injury and death are accidents a person thinks about ahead of time. Capture is an accident nobody expects, so you cannot learn one from the other.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tries a first answer, learning capture from injury and death, and then knocks it down right away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A borrower may accept responsibility for accidents he expects might happen, like injury or death. Capture is an unexpected accident, so maybe he never took it upon himself. That difference breaks the comparison.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you would say (bringing up a possible idea)
Let us learn (one case from another)
An accident that is out of one's control
Comes to mind, something a person expects
What about...? (pointing out a difference that breaks a comparison)

steps.confusionAlert: Both injury/death and capture are אונס (accidents). The difference here is not whether he was at fault. It is only whether people normally expect this kind of accident.

phrases.english: And if you would say, let us learn it from injured or died,
what about injured or died?
They are accidents that a person thinks might happen.
Will you say the same about captured,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁכֵּן אוּנְסָא דְּלָא סָלֵיק אַדַּעְתָּא הוּא!
phrases.english: which is an accident that a person does not expect?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a possible answer to the question in Step 27 and rejects it in the same breath.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The idea of learning capture from injury and death.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Injury and death are expected accidents, but capture is an unexpected one.

steps.title: Learning the borrower from the paid guardian
steps.stepSummary: Both the borrower's verse and the שומר שכר's verse say injured or died. The שומר שכר verse also says captured, so capture is applied to the borrower too.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather: injured or died is written about the borrower, and injured or died is written about the paid guardian. In the paid guardian's verse, captured appears with them. So here too, for the borrower, captured goes with them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new source. It links the borrower's verse to the paid guardian's verse because both use the same words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words שבורה ומתה appear in both passages. The שומר שכר passage also lists נשבה (captured). Because the wording matches, the גמרא carries capture over into the borrower's passage.

keyTerms.meaning: It was said, it is written

phrases.english: Rather: injured or died is written about a borrower,
and injured or died is written about a paid guardian.
Just as there, captured is included with it,
so too here, captured is included with it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The first idea failed in Step 28, so this gives a different source.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Because the borrower's verse and the שומר שכר's verse share the same words, capture (written for the שומר שכר) also applies to the borrower.

steps.title: The comparison to the paid guardian breaks down
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא attacks the comparison. For the שומר שכר, injured and died come to let him off, but for the borrower they come to make him pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: This can be knocked down. For the paid guardian, these words come to make him exempt. Can you say the same for the borrower, where they come to make him liable?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the source from Step 29 and shows a big difference between the two cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the שומר שכר passage, injured, died and captured are cases where he does not pay. In the borrower passage, injured and died are cases where he does pay. A passage that exempts cannot simply be used to add a case of paying.

keyTerms.meaning: It can be refuted, there is a hole in this comparison

steps.whatToRemember: Two sources for capture have now failed. Injury and death are expected accidents, and the שומר שכר's verse is about being exempt, not about paying. The next step gives a new source, רבי נתן's "או".

phrases.english: This can be refuted:
What about a paid guardian? There, these cases are stated to exempt him,
so can you say the same about a borrower, where they are stated to make him liable?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the source offered in Step 29.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The comparison between the borrower and the paid guardian.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: For the שומר שכר the words teach that he is exempt, while for the שואל they teach that he must pay, so one cannot be learned from the other.

steps.title: A new source for capture: the word "or"
steps.stepSummary: Capture is learned from רבי נתן, who says the word "או" in "injured or died" includes a captured animal.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, we learn it like רבי נתן, as a ברייתא teaches: רבי נתן says, the word "or" comes to include a captured animal.
steps.whatsHappening: The comparison to the שומר שכר just failed, so the גמרא offers a different source. It points to the small word "או" (or) in the borrower's verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The borrower's verse says "injured or died." רבי נתן reads the word "או" as adding another case, which is capture. Now capture comes from the borrower's own verse, so we no longer need the comparison that step 30 knocked down.

keyTerms.meaning: to include (a word in the פסוק adds another case)
captured (an animal taken away by raiders)

phrases.english: Rather, it is like Rabbi Natan,
as it is taught: Rabbi Natan says:
"Or" comes to include a captured animal.
phrases.notes: This is the "or" in "injured or died" in the borrower's verse, שמות 22:13.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the source that step 30 rejected with a new one.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Where do we learn that a borrower pays when the animal is captured? (from step 27)
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: From the extra word "או" in "injured or died," following רבי נתן.

steps.title: The word "or" is needed to separate the cases
steps.stepSummary: "או" is needed for something else: it shows that injury alone or death alone is enough. Without it we might think the borrower pays only when both happen.
steps.simpleTranslation: This "or" is needed to separate the cases. Otherwise you might think he is not liable unless the animal is injured and also dies. The word teaches us that this is not so.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי נתן's source. It says the word "או" already has a job, so it cannot also be used to add capture.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without "או," the verse could be read as one combined case: the animal was injured and then died. "או" tells us these are two separate cases, and either one makes the borrower pay. If the word is used up for this, nothing is left over to teach capture.

keyTerms.meaning: to separate; to show these are two separate cases

phrases.english: This "or"
is needed to separate the cases.
For it could enter your mind to say:
He is not liable until it is injured and dies,
so it teaches us otherwise.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks רבי נתן's source from step 31.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A word cannot be spare if it is needed for its plain job, and "או" is needed to make injury and death separate cases.

steps.title: Fine for רבי יונתן, but what about רבי יאשיה?
steps.stepSummary: The objection does not work for רבי יונתן, so "או" is free to teach capture. For רבי יאשיה it is still a problem.
steps.simpleTranslation: This works well according to רבי יונתן. But according to רבי יאשיה, what is there to say?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the objection for one opinion, רבי יונתן. Then it raises the problem again for the other opinion, רבי יאשיה. This line sets up a quote that will explain their argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יונתן, the verse would mean separate cases even without "או." So the word is extra and can teach capture. For רבי יאשיה, the verse would mean both together unless it is split, so "או" is needed to split it, and the question about capture comes back.

keyTerms.meaning: this works out well (according to one view)
what is there to say? (the problem remains)

phrases.english: This works out well according to Rabbi Yonatan.
But according to Rabbi Yoshiya,
what is there to say?

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנִיחָא לְרַבִּי יוֹנָתָן. אֶלָּא לְרַבִּי יֹאשִׁיָּה, מַאי אִיכָּא לְמֵימַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 32 for רבי יונתן, then renews the challenge for רבי יאשיה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי נתן's source for capture, according to רבי יאשיה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: For רבי יאשיה, "או" is needed to split injury and death, so it cannot also teach capture.
steps.confusionAlert: This line does two things at once: it settles the problem for רבי יונתן and reopens it for רבי יאשיה. Don't read "הניחא" as the end of the discussion.

steps.title: רבי יאשיה on cursing father or mother
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא shows רבי יאשיה's rule. "His father and his mother" alone would mean both together. Only the end of the verse, which splits them, teaches that cursing one parent is enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: As a ברייתא teaches: "A man who curses his father and his mother." From this I only know a case of both his father and his mother. Where do I learn the case of his father without his mother, or his mother without his father? The verse says: "His father and his mother he cursed." That means he cursed his father, or he cursed his mother. These are the words of רבי יאשיה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a ברייתא to show where רבי יאשיה's view comes from. This explains why רבי נתן's source is a problem for him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יאשיה, "father and mother" on its own means only both together. He needs the second half of the verse, where the curse is placed next to each parent, to learn that each one alone counts. The same reasoning means that "injured and died" needs "או" to make them separate, so for him "או" is not extra.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets out the basic disagreement between רבי יאשיה and רבי יונתן about how to read "and" in a פסוק. The question of whether רבי נתן's source for capture works depends on it.

phrases.english: As it is taught:

phrases.aramaic: ״אִישׁ אֲשֶׁר יְקַלֵּל אֶת אָבִיו וְאֶת אִמּוֹ״,
phrases.english: "A man who curses his father and his mother"
I only know of a case of his father and his mother together.
His father without his mother,
or his mother without his father, from where do we learn it?
The verse says: "His father and his mother he cursed."
He cursed his father, or he cursed his mother.
phrases.notes: The word "cursed" is near "father" at the start of the verse and near "mother" at the end, so each parent counts alone.

phrases.english: These are the words of Rabbi Yoshiya.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא: אִישׁ אֲשֶׁר יְקַלֵּל אֶת אָבִיו וְאֶת אִמּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Quotes the source for רבי יאשיה's view, which step 33 relied on.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי יאשיה, "father and mother" on its own means both together. Only the split wording of the verse teaches that cursing either parent alone makes a person liable.

steps.title: רבי יונתן: 'And' means both together and each one alone
steps.stepSummary: רבי יונתן says the phrase 'his father and his mother' covers cursing both parents together and also cursing just one of them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יונתן says: The phrase can mean both of them together, and it can also mean one of them by itself.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues with the other opinion. רבי יונתן says the word 'and' already includes each parent alone, so no extra source is needed for that.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יאשיה said 'and' alone would mean both together, so we need the end of the verse to split them. רבי יונתן says 'and' already carries both meanings at once. This is why, in step 33, 'או' was free for רבי יונתן to teach the captured animal, but not for רבי יאשיה.

keyTerms.meaning: It means / it can be understood as
One by itself, on its own

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two opinions. רבי יאשיה needs an extra word to split 'and'; רבי יונתן says 'and' already splits on its own.
steps.whyThisMatters: This opinion explains why, according to רבי יונתן, the borrower's 'או' can be used to teach the captured animal.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yonatan says:
It means both of them together,
phrases.notes: He is talking about the words 'his father and his mother' from the ברייתא in the step before.

phrases.english: and it means one of them on its own –

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן אוֹמֵר: מַשְׁמַע שְׁנֵיהֶם כְּאֶחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the second side of the ברייתא quoted in step 34, the opinion that disagrees with רבי יאשיה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי יונתן, the word 'and' in a פסוק includes both items together and each item alone, unless the פסוק says otherwise.
